In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the risk for HCC in cirrhosis is still high, and the challenge for chemopreventative trials is to identify the best target population and the most suitable treatment for the different risk factors.

the risk of hepatocarcinogenesis in patients with cirrhotic liver disease is not only dependent on the etiology, but also on the host genetic background and the environmental factors that may act as cofactors.
the identification of risk factors, the stratification of patients and the development of personalized chemoprevention algorithms are the key elements in the fight against HCC.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the development of chemopreventative agents is still in its infancy.
the risk of developing HCC is individualized, and that the design of successful chemopreventative strategies should take into consideration host, viral and other environmental risk factors.
the development of chemopreventives for HCC will be possible only after a careful evaluation of the individual risk of developing HCC.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the development of effective chemoprevention for HCC will require a better knowledge of the molecular mechanisms underlying HCC development and the identification of biomarkers that will allow us to select patients with the highest risk of tumor development.
the design of chemoprevention trials should be tailored to individual patient risk factors, and that a single agent approach may not be effective in reducing HCC incidence.

the development of HCC is the result of a complex interaction between host, viral and environment-related factors, that can be modulated with the use of antiviral treatments, but also by chemoprevention with drugs that are able to counteract tumor initiation, progression and/or metastasis.
